title: Array-as-queue
description: A plain array becomes a queue with push + shift — FIFO, but shift is O(n).

conversation.intro: How an interview about queue-as-array would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before reaching for a queue — pin down the access pattern.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I need a structure where items are processed in arrival order — first in, first out. That's a queue. Quick checks before I code:"

• Roughly how many items, and how often will I dequeue? Shift is O(n), so a million-element queue gets expensive.
• Do I need peek-at-front, or just push/shift?
• Is this for BFS, scheduling, or something else? (The classic use is BFS.)
• Any priority involved, or pure FIFO? (Priority queue = heap, not array.)
sections.why: Saying FIFO out loud is the magic word that names the abstract pattern. The 'how many items' question is the load-bearing one in JS — interview-scale (≤10⁴) is fine with `Array.shift`, but at production scale you'd reach for a head-pointer trick or a real deque. Asking it unprompted signals you've thought about the real complexity, not just the textbook complexity.

sections.title: 2. Why this template?
sections.prompt: Why an array, and what's the catch?
sections.say:
"In JS, a plain array can act as a queue: `push` to enqueue at the back, `shift` to dequeue from the front. That gives you FIFO. But there's a sharp edge: `shift` is O(n) because it re-indexes every remaining element after removing index 0. For interview-scale inputs it's fine; for huge queues you'd switch to a head-pointer pattern — keep an index `i` and never actually remove, just increment."

"Three idioms to know:"

• `queue.push(x)` — enqueue at back, O(1).
• `queue.shift()` — dequeue from front, O(n).
• `queue.length` — truthy drain condition: `while (queue.length) { ... }`.
sections.why: Flagging the O(n) shift cost unprompted is the senior-tier move — most candidates either don't know or don't mention it. The head-pointer fallback (`let i = 0; const front = q[i++];`) is the production answer; in an interview, naming it without implementing it signals depth without rabbit-holing.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern — when queues fire
sections.prompt: What problem signals say 'reach for a queue'?
sections.say:
"Three classic queue signals:"

• 'Process in arrival order' — task scheduling, request handling, replay of events.
• BFS / level-order traversal — the queue ensures you exhaust depth d before touching depth d+1, which is what gives BFS its shortest-path-in-unweighted-graphs guarantee.
• Producer/consumer streaming — items arrive over time, are consumed in order.

"For the L3 (`processQueue`), the pattern is the canonical 'copy + drain' shape: take the input, copy it into a queue so you don't mutate the caller's array, then `while (queue.length)` shift-and-process. The output array IS the FIFO order — for an already-arrival-ordered input, that just echoes the input, which is the whole point of demonstrating the pattern."
sections.why: Naming the three signals — and explicitly linking BFS to 'queue ensures depth-d before depth-d+1' — distinguishes derivation from pattern-matching. The 'copy + drain' framing is the template you'll reuse on BFS, on event replay, on any 'process this sequence in arrival order' problem.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: Three cases — the L3 prompt input, a single-element queue, and an empty queue. The single-item and empty-item cases prove the drain loop terminates correctly.

examples.note: The L3 case — typical input. Output echoes input because input was already in arrival order.
examples.trace:
Init: queue=['a','b','c'] (spread copy), out=[]
while (queue.length=3) → shift 'a' → out=['a'], queue=['b','c']
while (queue.length=2) → shift 'b' → out=['a','b'], queue=['c']
while (queue.length=1) → shift 'c' → out=['a','b','c'], queue=[]
while (queue.length=0) → exit
return ['a','b','c'] ✓

examples.note: Single element — one shift, drain complete.
examples.trace:
Init: queue=['only'], out=[]
shift 'only' → out=['only'], queue=[]
exit
return ['only'] ✓

examples.note: Empty input — drain loop never enters.
examples.trace:
Init: queue=[], out=[]
while (queue.length=0) → never enter
return [] ✓

sections.why: Echoing the input on example 1 is the moment the student often asks 'wait, what did the queue actually DO?' The answer: it demonstrated the FIFO drain pattern; the input was already FIFO so the output looks the same. The interesting case — where the queue's order matters — is BFS, which is one section away. Mentioning that the L3 is the simplest possible queue exercise (a 'syntax' lesson, not an algorithm) sets the expectation.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases & pitfalls
sections.prompt: What inputs or coding choices would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges and pitfalls worth flagging:"

• Empty input → drain loop never enters, returns the initial empty `out`. No special case needed.
• Mutating the caller's array → `[...items]` copies; doing `const queue = items` would have `shift` mutate the caller. The spread is load-bearing.
• Using `pop` instead of `shift` → you'd get LIFO output (reversed) and accidentally write DFS-style processing instead of BFS.
• Using `unshift + pop` to model a queue → also FIFO, but `unshift` is O(n) too, just moved to the enqueue side. No win.
• Huge queues (millions of items) → `shift` is O(n) per call, so the whole drain is O(n²). Switch to a head-pointer or a real deque (e.g. `denque` library, or a linked list).
sections.why: The 'pop reverses to LIFO and silently becomes DFS' point is the same trap as in BFS — naming it here ties the queue-as-array lesson to the BFS template. The head-pointer fallback for huge queues is the senior-tier touch: knowing when to break the idiom is worth more than knowing the idiom itself.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"For `processQueue` specifically: time is O(n²) because each `shift` is O(n) and we do n shifts. For interview-scale (≤10⁴) that's fine — it runs in milliseconds. For production-scale, swap to a head-pointer: `let i = 0; while (i < queue.length) { const x = queue[i++]; ... }` makes the whole thing O(n).

Space is O(n) — the spread copy and the output array both hold n items.

The template generalizes: BFS is `processQueue` with a step that ENQUEUES MORE work as you drain. Replace `out.push(queue.shift())` with `const cur = queue.shift(); for (const child of neighbors(cur)) queue.push(child);` and you've turned the drain into a level-by-level graph walk. Same primitive, more work per iteration."
sections.why: The 'O(n²) for the naive form' admission is what interviewers want to hear — too many candidates wave it away as 'O(n) because we shift n times' without acknowledging shift's cost. Linking `processQueue` to BFS as 'same scaffold, more work per iteration' is the transfer move that proves you see this as a template.

walkthrough.intro: Step through `processQueue` — the canonical copy-and-drain FIFO pattern. Watch the queue empty from the front while `out` fills in arrival order. Use ◀ Prev / ▶ Next, or pick a different example.

notes: push + shift gives FIFO, but shift is O(n) — fine for interviews, slow for millions.
For high-throughput queues, swap to a two-stack or head-index trick for amortized O(1).
When the problem says "process in arrival order" or BFS, reach for a queue.

questions.q: Which pair of methods turns an array into a queue?

options: Sorted by priority — highest priority dequeues first
Round-robin — items cycle back to the tail after each dequeue

questions.q: What is the time complexity of Array.prototype.shift on n elements?
options: O(1) — same as pop, since both remove a single element
Amortized O(1) — V8 uses a head-pointer optimization internally
O(log n) — the array's length is decremented via a balanced-tree-backed length property

questions.q: Which algorithm is the textbook use case for a queue?
options: In-order tree traversal — the queue holds the current ancestor path
Dijkstra's algorithm on weighted graphs — the queue orders nodes by distance

exercises.prompt: Enqueue "a", "b", "c" then dequeue twice and log the two results.
Count tree nodes using a queue-based BFS walk.

L3.prompt: Write `processQueue(items)` that copies items into a queue, drains it FIFO, and returns the drained order. Log `JSON.stringify(processQueue(["a", "b", "c"]))`.
hints: Spread the input into a fresh array.
While queue.length, shift the front and push to out.
